data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on Popper's terms as a rational choice based on 'verisimilitude' (truth-likeness) rather than probability, avoiding induction by treating corroboration as a report of past performance that informs the selection of the theory with the highest content and closeness to truth.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If verisimilitude cannot be formally defined without collapsing into probability or induction (as argued by Miller and Tich\u00fd).","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the preference implies an expectation of future success based solely on past performance.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If 'rational choice' inherently requires a probabilistic justification.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Popper distinguishes between the logical probability of a theory (which remains zero or low for high-content theories) and its verisimilitude. Corroboration does not increase probability but indicates that a theory has withstood severe tests, making it the best candidate for being closer to the truth than its rivals.
